clinicalPearls: IHD reflects an imbalance between myocardial oxygen supply and demand; the dominant cause is atherosclerotic narrowing of one or more epicardial coronary arteries reducing regional myocardial perfusion (Harrison 22e p.2090).

Anginal discomfort is classically described as heaviness, pressure, squeezing, smothering or choking rather than frank pain, is crescendo-decrescendo, typically lasts 2-5 minutes, and may be signaled by a clenched fist over the sternum (Levine's sign) (Harrison 22e p.2092).

Anginal pain may radiate to either shoulder, both arms (especially the ulnar forearm/hand), back, interscapular region, neck, jaw, teeth, or epigastrium; it is rarely localized below the umbilicus or above the mandible (Harrison 22e p.2092).
Radiation to the trapezius muscles is NOT typical of myocardial ischemia and points more toward pericarditis; this is a useful discriminating feature (Harrison 22e p.2092).

Anginal equivalents (dyspnea, nausea, fatigue, faintness) and atypical presentations are more common in women, the elderly, and patients with diabetes mellitus, in whom angina may not relate strictly to provoking factors (Harrison 22e p.2093).

A resting 12-lead ECG may be entirely normal in typical angina; ST-T and LVH changes are suggestive but nonspecific, whereas dynamic ST-T changes appearing with an anginal episode and resolving afterward are more specific (Harrison 22e p.2094).

A stenosis must reduce epicardial luminal diameter by about 50% to limit flow augmentation on demand, and by roughly 80% before resting flow falls; beyond that, small further reductions cut flow dramatically (Harrison 22e p.2091).
Reversible ischemic injury occurs within roughly 20 minutes of total occlusion (without collaterals); occlusion beyond 20 minutes leads to myocardial necrosis (Harrison 22e p.2091).
The Canadian Cardiovascular Society class grades angina severity and the New York Heart Association class grades functional limitation (Harrison 22e p.2093).

An ischemic stress-ECG response is flat or downsloping ST depression >0.1 mV lasting >0.08 s; upsloping or junctional ST changes are not diagnostic, and a test failing to reach 85% of age/sex-predicted maximal heart rate is nondiagnostic (Harrison 22e p.2094-2095).
Chest wall tenderness, pain reproduced by palpation, or pain localizable with a single fingertip makes a myocardial ischemic origin unlikely (Harrison 22e p.2093-2094).
Most patients who die suddenly from IHD do so from ischemia-induced ventricular tachyarrhythmias (Harrison 22e p.2092).
harrison.pathophysiology: Myocardial oxygen demand (MVO2) is governed by heart rate, contractility, and wall tension, while supply depends on oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood and coronary blood flow (predominantly diastolic). Coronary resistance resides mainly in prearteriolar (R2) and arteriolar/capillary (R3) microvascular beds, which normally dilate to match demand (metabolic regulation and autoregulation). Atherosclerosis of epicardial arteries, driven by endothelial dysfunction from high LDL, smoking, hypertension, and diabetes, produces subintimal plaques; plaque rupture or erosion exposes contents to blood, triggering platelet activation/aggregation and the coagulation cascade with fibrin deposition and thrombus formation. As proximal stenoses worsen, distal resistance vessels dilate maximally and flow becomes pressure-dependent, so increased demand (exertion, emotion, tachycardia) precipitates ischemia. Ischemia causes regional contractile dysfunction (hypokinesis to dyskinesis), impaired relaxation, a metabolic shift to anaerobic lactate production with falling intracellular pH and high-energy phosphate depletion, membrane dysfunction with potassium leak and cytosolic calcium rise, characteristic ECG repolarization changes, and electrical instability. The subendocardium is most vulnerable to underperfusion (Harrison 22e p.2090-2092).
additionalDifferentials: Aortic stenosis with severe LVH causing subendocardial ischemia and angina without coronary atherosclerosis (Harrison 22e p.2091)
Aortic regurgitation and pulmonary hypertension as causes of angina-like chest discomfort (Harrison 22e p.2093)
Microvascular angina / abnormal cardiac nociception in patients with ischemic-type chest pain but no flow-limiting epicardial obstruction, more common in women (Harrison 22e p.2093)
Vasospastic (variant) angina due to coronary spasm (Harrison 22e p.2091, 2093)
Pericarditis (suggested by discomfort radiating to the trapezius) (Harrison 22e p.2092)
Esophageal/gastrointestinal disease and musculoskeletal chest wall pain (Harrison 22e p.2093-2094)
nonInfectiousMimics: Chest wall / musculoskeletal pain reproducible on palpation
additionalInvestigations: Fasting lipid panel (total, LDL, HDL cholesterol, triglycerides, lipoprotein(a)) (Harrison 22e p.2094)
Glucose / hemoglobin A1c, creatinine, hematocrit; urinalysis including microalbuminuria; thyroid function if indicated (Harrison 22e p.2094)
High-sensitivity C-reactive protein (1-3 mg/L is an independent risk marker, most useful for reclassifying intermediate-risk patients) (Harrison 22e p.2094)
Chest x-ray for cardiac enlargement, ventricular aneurysm, or heart failure signs (Harrison 22e p.2094)
Exercise treadmill ECG stress testing (sensitivity about 75%) (Harrison 22e p.2094-2095)

Stress myocardial perfusion imaging (thallium-201 or 99m-technetium sestamibi SPECT) or PET (N-13 ammonia, rubidium-82) with exercise or pharmacologic (adenosine, dobutamine) stress (Harrison 22e p.2095)
Stress echocardiography and cardiac MR stress testing (Harrison 22e p.2095-2096)
Coronary artery calcium scoring (Agatston score) by EBCT/MDCT as adjunctive, not primary screening (Harrison 22e p.2095-2097)
Coronary CT angiography for intermediate pretest probability and plaque assessment (Harrison 22e p.2097)
Invasive coronary arteriography (with FFR/iwFR) per ISCHEMIA-informed indications (Harrison 22e p.2097-2098)
redFlags: Angina occurring with less exertion than before, at rest, or awakening the patient from sleep (features of an unstable syndrome) (Harrison 22e p.2093)
Angina accompanied by symptoms or signs of heart failure, pulmonary edema, transient third heart sound, or mitral regurgitation (Harrison 22e p.2092, 2097)
Inability to exercise beyond 6 minutes / stage II of the Bruce protocol (Harrison 22e p.2097)
Ischemia at low workload, >=0.2 mV ST depression, or ST depression persisting >5 minutes after exercise (Harrison 22e p.2097)
A fall in systolic blood pressure >10 mmHg during exercise or exercise-induced ventricular tachyarrhythmia (Harrison 22e p.2096-2097)
Large or multiple perfusion defects, increased lung tracer uptake, or a fall in LV ejection fraction during stress imaging (Harrison 22e p.2097)
Reduced resting LV ejection fraction (<0.40) (Harrison 22e p.2097)
Sudden cardiac death may be the unheralded presenting manifestation of IHD (Harrison 22e p.2092)
harrison.prognosis: Principal prognostic determinants are age, left ventricular function, the location and severity of coronary stenoses, and the severity/activity of ischemia. Recent-onset or unstable angina, early post-MI angina, angina poorly responsive to therapy, and angina with heart failure all carry increased risk. Elevated LV end-diastolic pressure/volume and reduced ejection fraction signal poor prognosis. Left main (>50% diameter) or proximal LAD obstruction carries greater risk than right or circumflex lesions because more myocardium is jeopardized. With any obstructive disease, mortality rises sharply when LV function is impaired; the larger the established necrosis, the poorer the prognosis. Conversely, patients with chest discomfort but normal LV function and normal coronary arteries have an excellent prognosis, as do those completing stage III of the Bruce protocol with a normal perfusion scan or negative stress echo. Greater number/severity of risk factors (advanced age >75, hypertension, dyslipidemia, diabetes, morbid obesity, peripheral/cerebrovascular disease, prior MI), elevated CRP, extensive coronary calcification, and increased carotid intimal thickening all worsen prognosis (Harrison 22e p.2097).
pitfalls: Relying on coronary artery calcium as the primary screening test or sole basis for therapeutic decisions; it is adjunctive only (Harrison 22e p.2092).

Interpreting a stress ECG without accounting for pretest probability; false positives rise in low-probability patients (e.g., asymptomatic men <40, premenopausal women without risk factors) and in those on digitalis/antiarrhythmics, with conduction disturbances, LVH, resting ST-T abnormalities, or abnormal potassium (Harrison 22e p.2095).
Assuming a negative stress ECG excludes CAD; sensitivity is only about 75%, though it makes three-vessel or left main disease unlikely (Harrison 22e p.2095).
Circumflex-territory disease may yield a false-negative stress test because the posterolateral wall is poorly represented on the surface 12-lead ECG (Harrison 22e p.2095).
Coronary arteriography images only the lumen and can miss severe non-luminal (remodeled, outwardly bulging) atherosclerosis (Harrison 22e p.2097).
Missing atypical/anginal-equivalent presentations in women, the elderly, and patients with diabetes (Harrison 22e p.2093).
Overlooking that about 25% of acute MI survivors never come to medical attention yet share the same adverse prognosis (Harrison 22e p.2092-2093).
harrison.severityClassification: Angina severity is graded by the Canadian Cardiovascular Society (CCS) functional classification (Class I: angina only with strenuous/rapid/prolonged exertion; Class II: slight limitation of ordinary activity; Class III: marked limitation with ordinary activity such as walking 1-2 blocks; Class IV: inability to perform any physical activity without discomfort, angina may be present at rest). Functional impact is described by the New York Heart Association (NYHA) classification (Classes I-IV) (Harrison 22e p.2093).
management: Antiplatelet therapy with aspirin, adding a second agent such as clopidogrel after acute events or revascularisation, together with a high-intensity statin to stabilise plaque and reduce cardiovascular events
Anti-anginal therapy with beta-blockers, calcium-channel blockers and long-acting nitrates to lower myocardial oxygen demand and relieve angina
Aggressive risk-factor modification: smoking cessation, blood-pressure and glycaemic control, and diet, exercise and weight optimisation
Coronary revascularisation by percutaneous coronary intervention or coronary artery bypass grafting for refractory symptoms or high-risk anatomy
Surveillance of lipids, glycaemic control, blood pressure and left ventricular function, with functional or anatomical ischaemia testing when symptoms change
Urgent treatment of acute coronary syndrome with antiplatelets, anticoagulation and timely reperfusion
Provide sublingual nitrate for acute angina and educate on warning symptoms that warrant emergency escalation
